title: Efficient Shapley-Based Influence Attribution in Social Networks

problem.claim: Fairly estimate the contributions of individual seed users before influence diffusion occurs.

gap.claim: Existing literature emphasizes seed selection, while ex-ante attribution without relying on single-run ex-post cascade logs remains underexplored.

contributions.claim: Introduces an ex-ante influence-attribution framework based on Shapley values to represent each seed's marginal impact.
Provides polynomial-time algorithms for single-step activation and proves #P-hardness for propagation beyond one step.
Develops approximation algorithms with provable guarantees for the standard IC model and time-bounded variants.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Empirical evaluation on real-world and synthetic networks demonstrates that the methods are efficient and effective.
The authors report that the methods offer a practical mechanism for ex-ante influence attribution.

narrative_sequence.summary: Social platforms rely on influence diffusion initiated by seed users.
The paper identifies the underexplored need to estimate individual seed contributions before diffusion.
The authors propose Shapley values for principled ex-ante influence attribution.
Stochastic diffusion and network dependencies create computational challenges.
The paper addresses the challenges with exact complexity results, approximation algorithms, and empirical evaluation.

source_observation.claim: Ex-ante attribution is motivated by uncertainty and the limited information in single-run cascade logs.

interpretation.claim: Attribution mechanisms can be designed to evaluate individual contributions before outcomes are observed.

application.claim: Such mechanisms may support budget allocation, influencer pricing, and privacy-preserving credit distribution.

exception.claim: Stochastic diffusion and network dependencies can make attribution computationally difficult.

source_observation.claim: The computational treatment differs between single-step and longer propagation processes.

interpretation.claim: Propagation horizon should influence whether exact or approximate attribution methods are used.

application.claim: Single-step settings can use polynomial-time algorithms, while standard and time-bounded models can use approximation algorithms with guarantees.

exception.claim: Propagation beyond one step is reported to be #P-hard.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the datasets, baselines, evaluation metrics, or quantitative results.
